bibliography.abstract: The risk of local arbovirus outbreaks in Europe is expected to increase due to climate change, as suggested by the multiplication of arbovirus outbreaks in the last decades. Europe has historically been a non-endemic region, making it vital to pinpoint which populations are potentially exposed -and under which conditions- so we can build truly robust epidemic preparedness capabilities. We introduce an integrated, multi-scale model that fuses a mechanistic transmission engine with a vector abundance framework, all embedded in a mobility-driven metapopulation system capturing human, vector, and air-traffic movement. To this end, we combine climate and population projections with mobility data to estimate and map dengue emergence risk in Europe throughout the 21st century. Additionally, we introduce a dedicated migration model that explores how climate-driven population redistribution could alter these risk estimates.Assuming the climate avoids major tipping points, model-derived risk indicators increase substantially under most emissions scenarios. While the spatio-temporal risk will remain largely driven by importation, our results indicate a gradual transition toward an environment-driven regime, particularly under the worst-case emissions scenario. To better anticipate and manage recurrent arbovirus outbreaks, our findings highlight the need to integrate mobility pathways and climate-driven population redistribution into predictive models of vector-borne disease emergence in temperate regions.
bibliography.title: Climate change and human mobility will shape dengue emergence risk in Europe

en.what: An integrated, multi-scale model was developed to project dengue emergence risk across Europe throughout the 21st century by combining a mechanistic transmission engine, a vector abundance framework, and a mobility-driven metapopulation system. The model incorporates climate projections, population forecasts, air-traffic data, and a dedicated migration model that accounts for climate-driven human redistribution. The simulations show a substantial increase in risk indicators under most emissions scenarios, indicating a gradual transition from import-driven transmission to an environment-driven regime under the worst-case emissions scenario.
en.why: The model establishes a quantitative link between climate-driven human migration and vector-borne disease transmission, providing a predictive capability to identify which European populations will face local outbreaks under shifting environmental conditions.
